State reported in 1960 PLD (SC) 387, Kaikaus, J has very elaborately spelt out the nature and corroboration which is required in a case of partisan or interested witnesses. In that reported decision it is found that there were 3 eye-witnesses of the occurrence of murder and the learned Sessions Judge believed all the 3(three) eye-witnesses. The learned Judges of the High Court felt that on account of partisan nature of the ocular, evidence it was necessary to consider whether the words of these 3(three) witnesses could be safely accepted against the accused persons in that case. In that reported decision the learned Judges accepted the corroborative evidence of Khairat Mahmud as true without any discussion of the circumstances which would point to the conclusion that the statement was true. The learned Judges just assumed the correctness of the statement and only considered the effect of its acceptance after accepting that the eye-witnesses are truthful witnesses. In that reported decision, the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of Pakistan on consideration of the evidence of the eye-witnesses found that the eye-witnesses were not truthful witnesses and in that view did not accept their testimonies and consequently, the question of corroboration was meaningless. The primary evidence of the eye-witnesses having been disbelieved by the Supreme Court of Pakistan the corroborative evidence was of no importance at all in the facts of that case. Kaikaus, J, in that decision observed as follows:</u>

<u>"The force that such circumstance should possess in order that it may be sufficient as corroboration must depend on the particular circumstance of the case. However the circumstance itself must be proved beyond all reasonable doubt. This rule of prudence requiring corroboration of partisan evidence has generally been accepted by Courts and was accepted by all the Judges of the Federal Court of Pakistan in Ashruf and others Vs. Crown (1) although the learned Judges were not in agreement as to what constituted corroboration".</u>

<u>66. In the case of Nazir and others Vs. State reported in 1962 PLD (SC) 269, Kaikaus, J in considering his observation made in that case of Niaz Vs. State observed as follows:</u>

<u>"This is what is meant by saying that the statement of an interested witness ordinarily needs corroboration. For corroboration it is not necessary that there should be the word of an independent witness supporting story put forward by an interested witness. Corroboration may be afforded by anything in the circumstances of a case which tends sufficiently to satisfy the mind of the Court that the witness has spoken the truth. What circumstances will be sufficient as corroboration it is not possible to lay down. But, as the question before the Court would be whether some innocent person had not been implicated in addition to those who were guilty the circumstance relied upon must have a bearing on this question. In the case of an interested witness the corroboration need not be of the same probative force as in the case of an accomplice for the two do not stand on the same footing".</u>

<u>In the present case the primary evidence of the eye-witnesses though interested and partisan was believed by the learned Judges of the High Court Division and along with it they also thought it necessary to seek for some corroboration. In fact from the evidence of PW 11 Kamalakshmi such corroboration as a circumstance leading to the presence of the appellants going away from the place of occurrence immediately after the occurrence was available. In the facts and circumstances of the present case and in the background of the rivalry and group faction between the parties the learned Judges of the High Court Division also found that no independent and disinterested witnesses were available. This being the position, the learned Judges found from the evidence of PW 11 Kamalakshmi as sufficient corroboration in the present case.</u>

<u>67. In the case of Karnail Singh and another Vs. State of Punjab reported in 1954 AIR (SC) 2 it was observed as follows:</u>

<u>"The corroboration that is required in such cases is not what would be necessary to support the evidence of an approver but what would be sufficient to "lend assurance to the evidence before them, and satisfy them that the particular persons were really concerned in the murder of the deceased. Vide —Lachhman Singh Vs. State 1952 AIR (SC) 167 at P 169(B), Karnail Singh was arrested on the spot with a spear and a bloodstained pyjama and these are pieces of evidence which would support the inference that he was concerned in the crime".</u>

<u>68. The same view has also been expressed in the case of Lachhman Singh and others Vs. State reported in 1952 AIR (SC) 167, wherein it was observed as follows:</u>

<u>"By adopting this standard the appellate Court does not condemn the oral evidence outright, but as a matter of prudence and caution it decides not to convict an accused person unless there were some circumstances to lend support to the evidence of the eye-witnesses with regard to him. The corroboration required is not that corroboration which one requires in the case of an approver or an accomplice, but corroboration by some circumstance which would lend assurance to the evidence before the Court and satisfy it that particular accused persons were really concerned in the offence".</u>

<u>Thus in the facts of the present case the learned Judges of the High Court Division believed the primary evidence of the eye-witnesses and having found support of the same from the corroborative evidence of PW 11 Kamalakshmi and the medical evidence on record upheld the conviction.</u>

<u>69. In the case of State of UP Vs. Pants Nath Singh and others reported in 1973 AIR (SC) 1073 it was observed as follows:</u>

<u>"There is no general rule that the evidence of the relations of the deceased must be corroborated for securing the conviction of the offender. Each case depends on its own facts and circumstances. In the present case the straight forward nature of the deposition of these two witnesses and the fact that they were undoubtedly in a position to identify the assailants of their father coupled with the recovery of blood stained earth from the place of occurrence leave no reasonable doubt about the guilt of the accused persons".</u>

70. Mr. Abdul Malek lastly submits that 36 persons were put on trial, out of which 10 were convicted by the trial Court and out of that only 4 accused were convicted by the High Court Division and this shows that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses have been disbelieved in respect of those accused persons and the same evidence should not have been relied upon to maintain the conviction of the present appellants.

71. I have already indicated above, that both the trial Court and the learned Judges of the High Court Division on consideration of the evidence on record did not think it proper to uphold the conviction of rest of the accused persons and ultimately gave benefit of doubt to them. Apart from defect of framing charge against three accused, benefit of doubt was given to the six accused persons as PW 11 Kamalakhsmi did not involve them in his deposition as found to have seen them going away from the place of occurrence soon after the occurrence. PW 11 Kamalakhsmi has involved these 4 appellants as going away from the place of occurrence. So, this additional circumstance was considered by the learned Judges of the High Court Division. The learned Judges were also not unmindful of the fact that for lack of corroboration from unrelated witnesses some of the accused were given benefit of doubt by the trial Judge and the State has not preferred any appeal against their acquittal order. Thus, I am of the view that the learned Judges have correctly considered the primary evidence of the eye-witnesses coupled with the available corroborative oral and medical evidences on record and upheld the conviction of these four appellants.

<u>72. It is not necessary for me to express any opinion on the point as to whether those accused were rightly acquitted or not. All that I can say is that the benefit of doubt which resulted in the acquittal of the other 6 accused could not vitiate the conviction of the 4 appellants as I find the evidence adduced against them is satisfactory and convincing. Further, I have already indicated that the appellants had strong motive to join in the killing, of these two deceased persons. The evidence about motive lends assurance to the evidence of the eye witnesses regarding the complicity of the appellants. I also find from the judgment of the High Court Division that the learned Judges took into consideration all other attending facts and circumstances of the case for maintaining the conviction of the appellants and also considered the following points in details in the judgment:</u>

<u>(a) That the FIR in this case was lodged at 12.30 and before the FIR the Deputy Commissioner, Superintendent of Police, Upazila Nirbahi Officer and other officers were present in the place of occurrence from 8-00 AM to about 10-00/11-00 AM and lot of people assembled there within half an hour of the occurrence. In the presence of top officers of the district and in view of this importance given by law enforcing agencies, the question of lodging of FIR did not at all assume any importance in the facts of the present case. Further, the First Information Report was lodged by not an eye-witness but by another nephew of deceased. In the occurrence two persons were killed and the FIR was filed in fact within 5 hours and in the circumstances as indicated above I do not think that any grievance can be made for not filing the FIR in time in the Police Station though the Police Station is close to the place of occurrence. Since, investigation had already started prior to the lodging of the First Information Report both the trial Court and the High Court Division correctly left the First Information Report out of consideration.</u>

<u>(b) That there being a strong motive and enmity between the parties, the learned Judges also correctly found that actuated by this the deceased were killed while going to Jessore to make tadbir in the murder case filed by the accused.</u>

<u>(c) That according to the prosecution the occurrence took place at 7-00 AM in the month of June, 1985. It is to be stated here that in the month of June even at 5-45 AM the sun is up and there is enough visibility to recognise persons. So it is not at all difficult from such close proximity on the part of these eye-witnesses to recognise the known persons at 7-00 AM particularly, PW 2 was surrounded at the scene of occurrence along with the deceased persons and was injured in the occurrence.</u>

<u>(d) That in this case deceased Eklasuddin and his son were murdered and the eye-witnesses were examined by the Police who saw the accused persons and as such no grievance can be made for not examining the female inmates of the house such as, wife and daughter of the deceased.</u>

<u>(e) That from the evidence of the police officer it is found that blood-stained earth along with empty cartridges were seized from the place of occurrence. 1 PW 18 Ballistic Expert deposed that he examined two single barrel 12 bore guns bearing No. 56 (made in England) and 60482 (made in Canada). According to his testimony, most probably 12 bore cartridge was fired from gun No. 56 which belongs to acquitted accused Lal Mia, but he is not sure about it and both the guns were in workable condition. The learned Judges took the view that appellant Nawabul Alam being a close relation of acquitted accused Lal Mia might have fired the gun from borrowing the same from his relation.</u>

<u>73. I have already indicated above that both the courts below have examined the evidence given by the eye-witnesses and have believed the said evidence. The learned Judges of the High Court Division accepted the evidence of the eye-witnesses as it appears to be very probable and natural. In such circumstances, it is not open to this court to re-assess the said evidence and decide whether the view taken by the High Court Division is right or not. In my opinion, the conviction of the four appellants rests on the appreciation of the oral evidence and other attending facts and circumstances of the case and hence no case has been made out for interference of this Division.</u>

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.

Order of the Court

By a majority decision the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order dated 18.3.91 of the High Court Division are set aside and the appellants are acquitted. Let the appellants be set at liberty forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case.
